## Study information

### Title

Prediction- (WP2) and intervention-arm (WP4) connection protocol:
definition of risk group at stage of child delivery

### Description

Globally, the prevalence of type 2 diabetes (T2D) is rising rapidly,
contributing to reduced life expectancy, lower quality of life, and
increased healthcare expenditure. In recent years, the development of
T2D has increased at alarming rates particularly among younger ages,
with epigenetic effects and prenatal exposures being critical
determinants. Pregnancy represents a period of metabolic vulnerability
due to the occurring physiological changes, where underappreciated
cardiometabolic risks can impact long-term maternal health and fuel the
intergenerational transmission of obesity and diabetes. Various adverse
pregnancy outcomes have been shown to be associated with increased
long-term risk of maternal and child cardiometabolic conditions.
Gestational diabetes (GDM) is one of the most common of such
complications, affecting around 6% of deliveries in Denmark. Despite
being historically recognized as a transient condition, GDM is now
established as an early marker of cardiometabolic disease, being
associated with a near tenfold higher risk of future T2D, as well as
cardiovascular disease, hypertension, and depression.\
Children of women with GDM, as well as pre-pregnancy obesity, and
increased gestational weight gain also have higher rates of obesity,
cardiovascular and cardiometabolic complications later in life, and it
is suggested that the impact of maternal obesity on childhood obesity is
independent of glycemic status.

In Denmark, currently used diagnostic criteria for GDM apply a very high
threshold, while they solely rely on a 2h plasma glucose value for GDM
diagnosis. Therefore, it is expected that many women who do not meet
this diagnostic threshold are still at elevated risk of reoccurring GDM
in a subsequent pregnancy and at elevated risk of T2D later in life.
Furthermore, there is a general impression that pregnancies and the
family formation stage are time points in the life course when women and
their families are more receptive to health messages and behavior
changes.

To date, the majority of literature exploring prevention strategies for
T2D focuses on prevention at the time when some degree of glucose
intolerance is already established. Recent evidence has highlighted the
need to shift perceptions by redesigning screening and intervention
approaches to follow a life course approach, instead of anticipating
abnormal glucose values to present. In this context, the work in DP-Next
intervention-arm (WP4) will be focused on reducing the risk of diabetes
in women who have recently given birth and their families. To identify
women at higher risk who will benefit from the intervention will be
based on connecting work with DP-Next prediction-arm (WP2).

## Objectives and hypotheses

### Definition of risk group for intervention work package (WP4) in prediction work package (WP2)

DP-Next prediction-arm aims to develop diabetes risk prediction models
for the entire population based exclusively on register-based data. The
aims and objectives of the work that will be carried out as part of the
DP-Next prediction-arm (WP2) is described elsewhere. (cite WP2 protocol)
This subproject for prediction-arm (WP2) will focus on calculating
diabetes risk specifically for women with a recent delivery, in order to
provide a clear selection of at-risk women that intervention group (WP4)
can focus on. An added benefit of focus on this specific group is that
various additional relevant variables are available for pregnant women
based on the registration of their first trimester pregnancy checkup. In
particular, BMI, smoking status, and blood pressure are recorded, as
well as measured HbA1c before or during pregnancy in many cases.

`#v(1fr)`{=typst}

::: box
The primary aim of DP-Next prediction-arm (WP2) is to: Develop and
validate a prediction model that identifies women at high risk of type 2
diabetes after the time of giving birth
:::

`#v(1fr)`{=typst}

Our long-term goal is to implement the model as a clinically ready tool
at the 8-week postpartum check-up in general practice, so that women at
high risk of type 2 diabetes can be offered timely initiatives designed
from intervention-arm (WP4) in DP-NEXT to improve cardiometabolic
health.

## Design plan for derivation of specific pregnancy-connected risk prediction model

### Study population (model derivation)

Prediction-arm (WP2) will derive the model for a cohort of women who:

Prediction-arm (WP2) will derive the model for a cohort of women who: -
Have given birth at least once between 2010 and 2015\
- Do not have a previous diagnosis of type 1 or type 2 diabetes at index
date\
- Stillbirths will be excluded exclusively for primiparous women
(parity=1) who experienced a stillbirth

### Time window for prediction

The index date is defined as one week after delivery, to ensure that all
delivery-related data have been recorded. Variables from the first
trimester through the delivery of child are therefore complete at the
index date. These data will be used for a potential use case at the
8-week postpartum check-up.

The model will predict the 10-year risk of registry-defined incident
type 2 diabetes (T2D). We chose a 10-year horizon because the population
is young, and few women will develop T2D within a shorter period. This
requires 10 years of potential follow-up from delivery. Registry data on
T2D incidence are available to the end of follow-up on 31 December 2025.
We therefore restrict the cohort to deliveries between 2010, when
laboratory data become available to some extent, and 2015, which allows
a full 10-year follow-up within the available registry data. Individuals
are right-censored by end-of-follow up, incedence of type 2 diabetes or
date of death.

If HbA1c data allow, secondary outcomes will be HbA1c levels at 5 and 10
years after the index birth, and HbA1c trajectories over this period.

### Definition of available data for prediction

The prediction models will be built based on general register-based data
supplemented with the results of the women’s first, second, third
trimester, and delivery based on data from the Medical Birth
Register(MFR). As the aim is to focus the intervention on the
post-partum period, risk indicators from pre-pregnancy and all pregnancy
stages as well as delivery can be incorporated into the risk model.

- Pre-pregnancy: based on pre-existing register-based data, following
  the same general-population strategy defined in WP2. It also includes
  additional information from previous deliveries.
- During pregnancy: additional data collected at the first, second, and
  third trimester pregnancy check-up.
- At delivery: additional data collected around the delivery and early
  health status of the baby.

All data come from Danish nationwide registries accessed through
Statistics Denmark (DST) and linked by the pseudonymised CPR number. The
index birth is identified in the Medical Birth Register, which also
links the woman to the child and to her earlier deliveries and
pregnancies, and the parent identifiers in the population register or
multi-generational registry (`MOR_ID`, `FAR_ID`) link her to her parents
and siblings for family history.

Pre-pregnancy predictors follow the WP2 strategy, using the population,
education and income registers, the National Patient Registry (LPR) and
the National Prescription Registry (LMDB), supplemented by earlier
deliveries in MFR. During pregnancy, MFR contributes BMI and smoking
from the first antenatal visit, while diagnoses and laboratory results
are placed in trimesters by their date. Delivery predictors come from
MFR and from the LPR records of mother and child.

Diagnoses from outpatient and emergency contacts and redeemed
prescriptions are available from 1995, so the 10-year look-back is
complete for index births from 2005 onwards. LPR changed data model from
LPR2 to LPR3 in February 2019, and both versions are combined. The
laboratory register reached nationwide coverage only in July 2015, so
laboratory-based predictors are available for a subset of index births
only. The registries and code systems (ICD-10 in the Danish SKS version,
SKS procedure codes, ATC, and NPU and local DNK codes) are summarised
below, and @tbl-predictors gives the source and codes for each
predictor.

: Available potential predictors in the National Registries

Codes are prefixes (DO14 covers DO14\*). ICD-10 codes are given in
Danish SKS format (D + ICD-10 code). The NPU lists are not exhaustive,
since laboratories also use local DNK codes; final lists should be built
from the `lab_forsker` code list inside the DST project. BEF, population
register; DST, Statistics Denmark; IND, income register; LMDB, National
Prescription Registry; LPR, National Patient Registry; MFR, Medical
Birth Register; OSDC, Open-Source Diabetes Classifier; RLRR, Register of
Laboratory Results for Research; SSSY/SYSI, Health Service Registry;
UDDA, education register.

Because the data sources in Table 1 differ in temporal and regional
coverage, we will develop the model in a main cohort using predictors
available nationwide for all index births. We will evaluate additional
predictors in sub-cohorts defined by the coverage of each partially
available source.

### Definition of cohort

In the full cohort, we will use all pre-pregnancy variables except
laboratory measurements.

- Explain demographic risk factors

- Explain diagnosis and prescription risk factors

- Explain family disease history risk factors

Nearly all pregnant women attend the scheduled antenatal visits, where
BMI and smoking status are recorded as standard in the first and third
trimesters. First-trimester BMI is minimally affected by gestational
weight gain and therefore approximates pre-pregnancy weight status, a
major determinant of type 2 diabetes. Smoking is associated with a
higher risk of type 2 diabetes, possibly through systemic inflammation
and central fat accumulation. In Denmark, an OGTT during pregnancy is
performed when risk factors for gestational diabetes are present. A
recorded OGTT therefore identifies women in whom gestational diabetes
was suspected, and both the test itself and a sub-threshold glucose
value may signal elevated risk of later type 2 diabetes.

We will further include variables recorded at and after delivery.
Gestational age at birth, mode of delivery and pregnancy complications
such as preeclampsia can be linked to maternal metabolic and vascular
health, and all are available at the postpartum check-up when the model
is applied. Neonatal anthropometry carries additional information.
Macrosomia, defined as a birth weight above 4000 g (or \> 4500 g), is
associated with elevated maternal risk of type 2 diabetes and may
reflect hyperglycaemia during pregnancy that screening did not capture.

#### Definition of subcohorts

In women with more than one pregnancy, the model is updated after each
birth, so that every birth contributes an index date. The model
integrates data from before, during and after each pregnancy and
predicts risk at the postpartum check-up. We will define subcohorts by
parity, so that women with a second or later birth contribute variables
from previous pregnancies as well as from the index pregnancy.

Availability of an HbA1c measurement before the index birth increases
over calendar time, from 10% of women in 2010 to 25% in 2015 and 40% in
2020. We will define a variable of women with a prior HbA1c measurement.
Because availability of laboratory measurements in the registries varies
by region over the period 2010 to 2015, we will restrict this subcohort
to the Central Denmark Region, the North Denmark Region, and the Capital
Region, where laboratory measurements are available.

Family history requires register linkage to relatives, and the number of
linkable relatives varies. Some women have relatives with relevant
records, such as an older sister with a previous pregnancy, whereas
recently immigrated women may have none. We will define subcohorts by
the availability of family linkage.

## Statistical methods

### Descriptive statistics

First, we will characterise the study population by demographic factors
(age, ethnicity, socioeconomic position) and by pregnancy related
factors from during the pregnancy and at delivery. Using the OSDC
algorithm, we will examine trends in the incidence of type 2 diabetes in
the population and across regions.

### Variable preprocessing

We will include predefined variables based on their established
association with the risk of type 2 diabetes, as listed in *Definition
of the potential predictors for prediction*. Diagnoses and medications
may carry hidden indications for type 2 diabetes risk; however, the
number of potential indicators is large. To select candidates for our
prediction model, we will create a play dataset based on a pregnancy
population from 2004 to 2010 to define the set of predictors. Women with
pregnancies after 2010 are excluded from the play data, to avoid
potential overfitting, i.e. we want the findings from the play data to
apply for the general population and not just the sub group we have data
on. We will include a 10 year history of each diagnosis and medication
and uniformly test the association between each diagnosis and each
medication and 10 year type 2 diabetes risk. We will produce a Manhattan
plot with groupings of ICD-10 and ATC codes on the x axis. We will bring
the candidates to domain experts in pregnancy related metabolic factors
from SDCA and SDCC and discuss: (1) whether the indications are biased;
and (2) the opportunity to collapse overlapping predictors (for example,
a diagnosis of hypertension together with a prescription for
antihypertensive medication). In a second step, we will estimate 10 year
risk diabetes for each person in the play data only given one of the
remaining variables from step 1. This will be repeated for each
remaining variable. We will then produce a plot with prevalence in the
population on the x axis and the magnitude of the association on the y
axis. In a second iteration with the domain experts, we will discuss the
relevance of each predictor based on prevalence of the diagnosis and
magnitude of risk. The candidates remaining after this discussion will
be included as candidate predictors for the main model.

### Statistical model selection

With the predictors defined in the play data together with the variables
defined in "Definition of available data for prediction", we will
continue to use the play data to select our candidate statistical
models. The dataset will be provided to the team of prediction
modellers, who will compete to create the best performing model while
remaining methodologically available to each other. As the primary
outcome, the model will aim to predict events of type 2 diabetes and, if
the data allow, to predict 5 year HbA1c levels after pregnancy. The
methods available for the modellers to choose from could include Cox
proportional hazards, Poisson regression, LASSO, and random forest, each
of which could be applied separately or combined in a super learner. The
candidate models selected on the basis of this step will then be brought
to the development dataset.

### Developing prediction model

Once all predictors and statistical models have been defined, we will
train the models on data from pregnant women enrolled between 2010 and
2014 in the full cohort. To handle partial marker availability in the
cohort, we will use three approaches.

Developed in the full cohort

1)  Include the variable as a present/absent indicator together with
    calendar time

2)  Multiple imputation of markers available at baseline, integrated
    into the full cohort.

Developed in the defined subcohort

3.  A submodel restricted to complete cases in the subcohort.

All models will be included in a super learner, which will select the
best-performing model by cross-validation based on the Brier score.

### Validation

For validation, we will use two approaches: first, we will subset one
region from the development dataset to test performance across regions;
second, we will subset the latest year (2015) to test performance on
newer data, which will reflect the situation when the model is deployed
on the 2027 population. Predictive performance will be assessed by the
Brier score to emphasize on individual calbraition of risk. We will
subdivide and test performance across age-groups, parity, and HbA1c
present or absent at baseline.

### Choosing and creating the final prediction model

The best performing model from the super learner will be trained on data
from the entire period from 2010 to 2015 and exported from the protected
environment it was developed in. It will then be built into an R Shiny
app, which will be provided to the group in WP4. Our model will provide
an estimate of the 10 year risk of type 2 diabetes and the expected 5
year HbA1c after pregnancy. Our approach follows established principles
in machine learning and statistical modeling, adhering to standardized
practices for prediction, reporting, and validation [@collins2024;
@lopez-ayala2025; @collins2024a; @riley2024].

## Definition of focus group for intervention-arm (WP4)

After the pregnancy risk model has been developed, it can be run for
more recent age cohorts, and an up-to-date descriptive analysis can be
made of the distribution of long-term T2D risk among recently pregnant
women. This descriptive analysis will show which data are most
informative for the estimation of future diabetes risk. It can also be
used to explore geographical variation and clustering of risk factors.
WP4 can then choose a more focused group of high-risk women in the
postpartum period, and geographical settings. It may be worth
considering focusing on GPs that measure HbA1c routinely in pregnant
women (improved risk prediction), and on women above a given BMI
threshold.
